blocks.text: 1. Versioning

blocks.alt: Knowledge base v1 leads to v2, then v3

blocks.text: Incremental Indexing closed by requiring a vector and its metadata to be inserted together atomically. Versioning, tracking changes to the knowledge base over time so they can be inspected or rolled back, adds the missing safety net for when an incremental update actually goes wrong.
It tags every indexed document with a version identifier rather than silently overwriting the old one.
2. Overwriting Versus Preserving History
A naive update overwrites the old chunk with the new one, losing the previous version entirely.
Versioning instead preserves the old version alongside the new one.

blocks.text: 3. Why A Knowledge Base Change Would Ever Need Reverting

blocks.alt: A bad update triggers reverting to a previous version

blocks.text: A faulty ingestion run can insert wrong or corrupted content into the live index.
Without a previous version to fall back to, undoing that mistake means starting over.
4. Version Identifiers Need To Be Explicit

blocks.alt: A document carries an explicit version ID

blocks.text: As with the cache key must include the model version in Embedding Cache, a document without an explicit version tag cannot be distinguished from its earlier self.
Every indexed document needs its version recorded as real, queryable metadata.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Two copies of the same document with no version tag, look identical to the system even though one is outdated, unless a version identifier is stored alongside them as queryable metadata.

5. Versioning At The Document Level Versus Collection Level

blocks.alt: Document-level versioning is compared against collection-level versioning

blocks.text: As with knowledge graphs versus relational tables in Knowledge Graphs, tracking one document's version differs from tracking a version for the entire indexed collection.
A full collection version captures a consistent snapshot across every document at once.

blocks.text: 6. Rolling Back To A Previous Version

blocks.alt: The current version rolls back to a previous version

blocks.text: A rollback restores retrieval to a previously known-good version instead of the current, faulty one.
This is only possible because that earlier version was actually preserved, not overwritten.
7. Versioning Answers The Response Cache Key Problem

blocks.alt: A version ID becomes part of the response cache key

blocks.text: As with the response cache key must include the retrieved context in Response Cache, a response cache needed a way to detect that the retrieved context had changed.
A version identifier is exactly the signal that response cache key was missing.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: The response cache key needing to reflect the retrieved context is satisfied directly by including the document or collection version identifier in this topic, closing that earlier open question.

blocks.text: 8. Keeping Every Version Forever Is Expensive
Storing every historical version indefinitely grows storage without bound.
Versioning needs its own retention policy, keeping only a bounded, useful history.
9. Recognizing When Explicit Versioning Is Worth Its Storage Cost

blocks.alt: Needing rollback capability points toward explicit versioning

blocks.text: A knowledge base with real risk of bad ingestion runs needs explicit versioning.
A small, manually reviewed knowledge base may tolerate simpler, unversioned updates.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates versioned document updates with a rollback to a previous known-good version.

code.content:
version_history = {}

def update_document(doc_id, content):
    # overwriting versus preserving history
    history = version_history.setdefault(doc_id, [])
    new_version = len(history) + 1
    history.append({"version": new_version, "content": content})
    return new_version

def get_current_version(doc_id):
    return version_history[doc_id][-1]

def rollback(doc_id, target_version):
    # rolling back to a previous version
    history = version_history.get(doc_id, [])
    for entry in history:
        if entry["version"] == target_version:
            history.append({"version": len(history) + 1, "content": entry["content"], "rolled_back_from": target_version})
            return f"Rolled back to version {target_version}, now stored as version {len(history)}"
    return "Target version not found"

v1 = update_document("doc1", "The Falcon plan costs twenty dollars per month.")
v2 = update_document("doc1", "The Falcon plan costs a corrupted, wrong value.")

print(f"Current version: {get_current_version('doc1')}")

result = rollback("doc1", v1)
print(f"\n{result}")
print(f"Current version after rollback: {get_current_version('doc1')}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows a faulty second version being rolled back to the first, known-good version, exactly the recovery as why a knowledge base change would ever need reverting.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Overwriting documents in place with no way to recover a previous, known-good version.
Storing documents without an explicit, queryable version identifier.
Confusing document-level versioning with a full collection-level consistent snapshot.
Keeping every historical version forever with no retention policy bounding storage growth.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Versioning tracks changes to the knowledge base over time so they can be inspected or rolled back.
A naive update overwrites the old version; versioning preserves it alongside the new one.
A faulty ingestion run can insert wrong content, and versioning is what makes reverting it possible.
Every indexed document needs an explicit version identifier stored as queryable metadata.
Document-level versioning differs from collection-level versioning, which snapshots everything at once.
A rollback restores retrieval to a previously known-good version, only possible because it was preserved.
A version identifier is exactly the signal a response cache key needs to detect changed context.
Storing every version forever grows storage without bound, requiring its own retention policy.
